Most people judge crypto payments solutions on how easy it is to spend stablecoins.

That part’s kinda solved now.

You can tap a crypto card at a restaurant and the waiter has no idea anything’s different. 

Behind that tap your money gets converted and routed so the restaurant gets paid, and you never think about it.

I wouldn’t be surprised if crypto neobanks become one of crypto’s next big product-market fits.

But what I keep thinking about is what your money’s doing the rest of the time. Like…most of it just sits there until you need to pay someone.

One project working on that is @veloprotocol, and they’re not starting from zero.

• Their Lightnet network runs that behind-the-scenes stuff across 150 countries, with 17 financial licenses and around $20B a year in volume as of 2025.

• Then there’s Orbit+, their wallet. You keep your own keys, pay with stablecoins, swap between chains in one click through SquidRouter, cash out to your bank, and there’s a card.

The part I actually find interesting is what’s NEXT. 

Velo is exploring Telegram payments, AI-agent payments, and even treasury tools that could let businesses earn yield on idle funds while keeping that money available for payments.

Imagine your business funds earning yield until you actually need to pay someone.

That's a pretty interesting direction for financial apps to take.

Of course, much of that is still on the roadmap, and actual adoption matters. 

But I think the next generation of crypto neobanks will have to offer more than just an easy way to spend stablecoins.

If someone makes that feel normal for regular people, I think it’s a much bigger deal than another card launch.

$NKE case study

One of the most important lessons I’ve learned throughout my investment career, often through my own failures trying to catch falling knives, is that you should never buy a stock simply because it has fallen significantly or because it looks cheap.

Take $NKE, for example. The business has been struggling for years, and the stock has reflected that. So why buy it?

The answer cannot simply be that it’s cheap or that it’s down 50%.

You need a reason to believe something is going to change.

Maybe you’ve visited Nike stores, studied the new product lineup, or noticed improvements that the market hasn’t fully recognized yet. Whatever it is, you need a thesis for why the future will be different from the past.

This applies to every stock.

The current price already reflects the market’s collective expectations. Your edge comes from identifying something that could change those expectations.

A stock being cheap is not an investment thesis. A stock being down 50% is not a catalyst.

You don’t buy because something has gone wrong. You buy because you have a reason to believe something is about to go right.

Podcasts, TV shows, and seemingly everyone on Wall Street and X were celebrating Leopold Aschenbrenner as the new wunderkind, the genius who had supposedly figured out Wall Street and the future of AI.

Now, with hindsight, it’s easy for everyone to see the risks. But at the time, I was almost the only voice on X warning people to be extremely careful with this guy. His returns seemed astronomical, almost illogical. Something about the numbers simply didn’t add up.

For saying that, I received countless hate messages telling me how stupid I was, that I didn’t understand his genius, and that I was simply jealous of his success. Interestingly, looking back at my original post now, I see that most of those comments have conveniently been deleted. Typical X behavior.

I’m not jealous of anyone’s success. I wish everyone great success. But one thing I’m very good at is recognizing patterns.

Only in hindsight did we discover the extraordinary leverage behind those returns. Reports indicated that his fund was borrowing as much as $3 to $4 for every $1 of capital. What appeared to be extraordinary investment genius was also extraordinary risk-taking.

Back in 2013 I was living in Spain, watching banks across southern Europe fail one after another. The European debt crisis was in full swing and it got bad enough that I bought a generator and filled the cupboards with tinned food.

Then Cyprus did something no country had done before. Its banks were going under, and instead of rescuing them, the authorities made the depositors pay... anything over €100,000 in your account was swapped for shares in a collapsing bank. They called it a bail-in. People lost their savings overnight.

That was the moment it dawned on me... you don’t actually own the money in your bank account. The bank does. And it can do what it likes with it.

So I went looking for somewhere to keep money that nobody else had a claim on, and that search led me to Bitcoin. I bought my first at around $200.

It started as my escape hatch from a broken banking system and eventually I understood it as the life raft out of the debasement trap.

It’s where the crypto chapter of The Everything Code picks the story up... with a generator and a cupboard full of tinned food.

AI data-centre: 100% moratorium improbable, modest slowdown likely and it will elongate the cycle (and the selloff has already priced a lot in)

Post-midterm noise has focused on local ballots, state pauses and talk of tighter rules on new data centres. Legitimate friction exists: power, water, permitting and community pushback are real constraints. However, a near-total U.S. halt is improbable as it will send the US into an immediate recession.

AI is a strategic priority; economic and geopolitical costs of freezing buildout are high. Much near-term capacity is already permitted or under construction.

Private land + evolving power solutions (gas, nuclear, efficiency) + international options provide outlets.

No federal ban has material traction; impact is more delay and higher cost than cancellation.

Base case from banks: some 2028 projects slide to 2029. This elongates the AI capex cycle rather than derailing it. Positives include:

1) Smoother supply-demand rebalancing (less boom-bust risk for the supply chain).

2) Better utilisation and pricing power for compute.

3) Improved credit outlook and more sustainable multi-year spending.

4) Hyperscalers still guiding strong near-term capex; and they will likely become FCF +ve

The aggressive selloff in AI infrastructure names (picks-and-shovels, semis, related industrials) has already discounted substantial slowdown risk. Multiples have compressed hard while order books and guidance have stayed firm. This looks more like a positioning/sentiment reset than a fundamental end of the cycle.

Quality AI infrastructure exposure still looks attractive if demand holds. Best to own companies with strong balance-sheets, high margins, FCF and real backlog. https://t.co/YKr5pL7G2c
